summary: Considers how Differentiated Services interacts with IP tunnels of various forms. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Priority labels on packets can get confused when packets are wrapped inside others. This discusses how to handle that.

questions: what is diffserv over a tunnel
uniform model vs pipe model diffserv
does dscp copy to the outer ip header
subtitle: How priority markings on packets should behave when packets are wrapped inside another IP header.

tldr.problem: A tunnel adds a second IP header, so a packet carries two DSCP values, and the diffserv architecture gave tunnel designers incomplete guidance on what to do with them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes a uniform model and a pipe model, and proposes doing traffic conditioning in series with tunnel encapsulation and decapsulation, with a static choice of inner or outer DSCP at the egress.
tldr.outcome: Tunnel designers get a simpler set of rules, with IPSec tunnels constrained by security to select the inner DSCP at egress.

today: RFC 2983 is an Informational memo from October 2000 and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It builds on the diffserv architecture in RFC 2475.

sections.title: Tunnels and the DSCP
sections.content:
An IP tunnel wraps traffic in another IP header. The inner header belongs to the original traffic, and the outer header is attached at the tunnel ingress and removed at the egress. Nodes in between look only at the outer header, so diffserv nodes read and change the DSCP in the outer header only. The memo treats tunnels as unidirectional and considers IP tunnels only, not MPLS paths or link-layer encapsulation.

The DSCP in the outer header may be modified between ingress and egress, and it may be desirable to copy it to the outer header on entry or back to the inner header on exit. The diffserv architecture offers incomplete guidance. Some PHB specifications followed its Guideline G.7 by naming the PHBs allowed in the outer header, which is overly restrictive. The memo prefers describing the behavioral properties of a PHB worth preserving and letting the outer header be marked in any way that keeps them.
sections.eli5: A wrapped parcel has two labels, inside and outside. The post office in the middle only reads the outside one, so we need rules for how the two labels should agree.

sections.title: The Uniform and Pipe Models
sections.content:
In the uniform model, a tunnel is just part of the path. Only the DS field in the outermost header counts. Implementations copy the DSCP to the outer header at encapsulation and copy the outer DSCP back to the inner header at decapsulation, so tunnels can be configured without regard to diffserv domain boundaries.

In the pipe model, the tunnel hides the nodes between ingress and egress. The egress uses the DSCP in the inner header and discards the outer one. If ingress and egress are in different diffserv domains, the egress must condition traffic so exiting DSCPs suit its own domain, though a Traffic Conditioning Agreement between the domains can reduce that work. The pipe model also helps when the DSCP carries information through the tunnel, such as AF drop precedence that would be lost on a path using the EF PHB.

If only one end is DS-capable, either model can be applied to the part of the tunnel inside that domain. If only the ingress is DS-capable and the outer DSCP is discarded, the ingress must set the inner DSCP to something the egress network accepts. The value 0 is used by a number of tunnel implementations, and class selector codepoints can work where IP precedence (RFC 791) is supported.
sections.eli5: Uniform: the outside label and inside label are kept the same, so everyone treats the parcel one way. Pipe: the inside label is a secret message that is only read at the far end, ignoring whatever the outside label became.

sections.title: Ingress: Where to Condition Traffic
sections.content:
The memo's approach keeps traffic conditioning in series with the tunnel, not in parallel, so no extra path carries information across a tunnel endpoint. IPSec requires this to keep its security properties. It yields three places to condition traffic around encapsulation: Before, Outer and Inner.

Before and Outer are independent of the tunnel and should be allowed. Inner is hard to use because it must reach inside the packet, which is impossible for encrypted or integrity-protected tunnels like IPSec. The main exception is a DS-incapable egress that discards the outer header, where the inner DSCP must suit the egress network.

Where reordering matters, such as IPSec with anti-replay or L2TP configured to restore ordering, the traffic through a tunnel should be marked at Outer as a single ordered aggregate. For different reordering behavior, use multiple parallel tunnels between the same endpoints. Service provisioning policies decide which flows use which tunnel, so EF traffic should not go through an inadequately provisioned Default tunnel.
sections.eli5: You can fix the markings before wrapping or on the outer wrapper, but not on the sealed inside. If a delivery lane must keep parcels in order, put them all in the same lane.

sections.title: Egress: Choosing the DSCP
sections.content:
At decapsulation, two DSCPs are reduced to one, which can lose information. Letting traffic conditioning use both would need the outer DSCP as an out-of-band input and complicate the model. So the memo recommends that tunnels support static selection of either the inner or the outer DSCP at egress, and leave full traffic conditioning to the Outer location (before decapsulation) and the After location (afterward). Usually only one of the two values carries useful information: the outer for uniform-model tunnels, the inner for pipe-model tunnels.

IPSec tunnels are usually pipe-model and, for security reasons, are currently required to select the inner DSCP. They should not select the outer one without an adequate security analysis.

A case study considers AF groups at both ends with a middle domain that uses IP precedence and receives the DSCP set to zero. The egress can reselect the AF group but cannot rebuild the lost drop precedence, although it can construct new markings. The memo judges that this benefit does not justify the added complexity of exposing both DSCPs to traffic conditioning.
sections.eli5: When you unwrap, pick one label to keep, the inside one or the outside one, and decide that ahead of time. It is simpler than trying to blend both.

sections.title: Translators and Security
sections.content:
Protocol translators, such as those using the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm, are not tunnels because they add no second IP header. But a translation boundary is likely also a diffserv domain boundary, so translators should allow edge-node processing, including traffic conditioning, both before and after translation.

On security, the diffserv security considerations still apply to tunnels. A tunnel egress in the interior of a domain acts as the DS ingress node for exiting traffic and must condition it against theft and denial-of-service threats. The IPSec architecture adds that the outer header is to be discarded unless the properties of the traffic conditioning to be applied are known and analyzed for vulnerabilities.
sections.eli5: The exit door of a tunnel must check what comes out, because a cheater could mark packets as more important than they are.
